newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-ASEAN takes stand against speculators.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-ASEAN takes stand against speculators.

text.p: Southeast Asian nations, racked by a series of speculative attacks on their currencies, on Friday pledged to tighten cooperation amongst themselves to combat the problem.

The Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) wrapped up its two-day ministerial meeting with a statement expressing "serious concerns" over "well coordinated efforts to destabilise ASEAN currencies for self-serving purposes, thus threatening the stability of all ASEAN economies".

The foreign ministers seemed to be echoing words from Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, who a day earlier delivered a searing condemnation of "rogue speculators" whom he accused of deliberately plotting to undermine the region's economies.
The ASEAN statement stopped short of proposing any concrete solutions or laws, but called for "further intensification of ASEAN's cooperation to safeguard and promote ASEAN's interests".
Ministers left no doubt about the seriousness of their intent: the section of the closing statement discussing the currency coordination was headlined "International Currency Manipulation".

"We did not make any specific resolutions on this in terms of what we need to do specifically," Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi told reporters following the ministerial meeting closing ceremonies.
Abdullah said the foreign ministers decided to leave such specifics to their finance ministers and central bankers.

The clamour over the region's currency woes was stoked by Mahathir on Thursday when the Malaysian premier, not known for mincing his words, made the currency speculation issue a highlight of his keynote address to ASEAN ministers. He said ASEAN may consider laws to curb such activities.
Although the ministerial meetings are a political venue, the bashing of Southeast Asia currencies in the past few weeks has been an unavoidable topic.

Thailand's economic crisis triggered a devaluation of its baht after heavy speculative attacks. The Philippines peso suffered similarly, and central banks in neighbouring Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore have been busy protecting their turfs.

The region's central banks have agreements to help each other during currency crises, but the ASEAN statement on Friday was the first coordinated public stand against currency marauders. In part, that was because the meetings offered an opportunity for senior ministers to share their thoughts on the situation.

"All the foreign ministers whose countries have suffered as a result of currency manipulation were here and we expressed concern over what has happened. It was very important that we expressed our concerns collectively," Abdullah said.
The decision to take a common stand against speculators comes after individual actions by the affected countries that have had mixed results.
Thailand imposed capital controls, while Malaysia's central Bank Negara Malaysia has said it will take unspecified stern measures against those who manipulate its currency.
The currencies of both countries along with those of Singapore, Indonesia and the Philippines have continued to be pressured even after Mahathir's strongly worded speech.

"If we (ASEAN) can do it (protect our currencies) together, it would be better than having individual measures and strategies...because there's a very strong link between members of the ASEAN economies," Abdullah told reporters.

ASEAN consists of Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam plus Burma and Laos, which were admitted this week. Cambodia's membership was postponed indefinitely due to its political troubles.
